sections.title: Weight and g on other bodies

parts.title: Why g is different
parts.html:
Weight is the force of gravity on an object: $W = m \times g$. The mass $m$ is the amount of matter and is the same everywhere. The gravitational field strength $g$ is the force per kilogram at that place, and it is different on each body.

$g$ at the surface of a body depends on the body's mass (more mass → stronger pull) and its radius (further from the centre → weaker pull). The Moon has about 1/80 of the Earth's mass but only about 1/4 of its radius, which works out at $g \approx 1.6$ N/kg — about a sixth. Jupiter is far more massive, so even with its large radius $g$ is about 25 N/kg.

Bodyg in N/kgWeight of 60 kg
Earth10 (9.8)600 N
Moon1.696 N
Mars3.7222 N
Jupiter251500 N

A newton meter (spring balance) reads the weight, so it reads less on the Moon; a beam balance compares masses, so it reads the same. Gravity does not stop in orbit: $g$ is a little smaller at the height of the ISS (about 8.7 N/kg), and that gravity is what keeps it in orbit (N4).

parts.title: Weight on Mars
parts.question: A lander has a mass of 1200 kg. On Mars $g = 3.7$ N/kg. Calculate the lander's weight on Mars and compare it with its weight on Earth.
steps: Equation: $W = m \times g$
Working: $W = 1200 \times 3.7$
Units: N on Mars — on Earth it is $1200 \times 10 = 12\,000$ N; the mass is 1200 kg in both places

questions.model:

  • …because the Moon has much less mass than the Earth (and a smaller radius), so its gravitational pull on each kilogram is weaker.

sections.title: Orbits: moons, planets, comets and artificial satellites

parts.title: The four kinds
parts.html:
BodyOrbitsShape and speed
Planets (and dwarf planets, asteroids)the Sunnear-circular (slightly elliptical) orbits, all in roughly the same plane and the same direction; speed almost constant; the further out, the slower and the longer the year
Moons (natural satellites)a planetnear-circular; the Moon takes about 27 days
Cometsthe Sunhighly elliptical: far out for most of the orbit, then a fast swing round the Sun; fastest when closest to the Sun, slowest when furthest; grow a tail near the Sun

parts.title: Choosing a satellite orbit
parts.question: Explain why a satellite used to relay television signals is put in a geostationary orbit, while a weather satellite is put in a low polar orbit. (3 marks)
steps: Geostationary: its period is 24 hours, the same as the Earth's rotation, so it stays above the same point on the equator — a fixed dish on a roof can point at it permanently.
Polar, low: it circles every ~90 minutes while the Earth turns beneath it, so over a day it passes over the whole surface and can photograph everywhere.
Height: a low orbit is also closer, so the images are more detailed.

sections.title: Circular orbits: changing velocity at constant speed

parts.title: Velocity changes, speed does not
parts.html:
Velocity is a vector: speed and direction. In a circular orbit the speed is constant but the direction is changing continuously, so the velocity is changing, so the planet is accelerating — towards the centre. An acceleration needs a resultant force, and that force is gravity, acting towards the Sun, at right angles to the velocity. Because it is at right angles it does no work: it changes the direction of the motion but not the speed.

The June 2024 marks (Q9(a)): the resultant force on a body in circular motion points towards the centre (not along the motion, no vertical component for a horizontal circle); it is accelerating because "its direction is continuously changing" or "there is a resultant force" or "velocity is a vector". "Centripetal force" on its own was ignored.

Speed and radius (7.7P, qualitative): for a stable orbit the gravitational force must be exactly enough to keep bending the path into a circle. Closer to the Sun gravity is stronger, so the orbit must be faster; further out it is weaker, so the orbit is slower. Put the other way: if the speed of an orbiting body increases, it must move to a smaller radius to stay in a stable orbit; if it slows, to a larger one. That is why Mercury races round in 88 days and Neptune takes 165 years.

parts.title: The 3-mark explanation
parts.question: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Explain why its velocity is changing and what causes the change. (3 marks)
steps: Velocity is a vector, with direction as well as size; in a circle the direction is continuously changing, so the velocity changes even though the speed does not.
A changing velocity is an acceleration, which needs a resultant force.
That force is gravity, acting towards the centre of the Earth, at right angles to the velocity — so it changes the direction but not the speed.

questions.text: A planet orbits the Sun at constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating. (2)
questions.model:
• Its direction is continuously changing, and velocity is a vector, so its velocity is changing.
  • A change in velocity is an acceleration (there is a resultant force — gravity — towards the Sun).

questions.text: In which direction does the force of gravity act on a planet in a circular orbit?
questions.explain: Towards the centre, at right angles to the velocity.

questions.text: Explain why the force of gravity changes a planet's velocity but not its speed. (2)
questions.model:
• Gravity acts towards the centre, at right angles to the velocity.
  • A force at right angles to the motion changes the direction (bends the path) but does no work along the motion, so the speed stays the same.

questions.text: Two satellites are in stable circular orbits. Satellite X moves faster than satellite Y. Which is correct?
options: X has the smaller orbital radius
X has the larger orbital radius
Speed and radius are not linked
questions.explain: A higher speed needs a stronger gravitational pull to hold the circle, which means being closer in.

questions.text: Mercury orbits the Sun faster than Neptune. Explain why, in terms of gravity. (2)
questions.model:
• Mercury is much closer to the Sun, so the gravitational force on it is much stronger.
  • A stronger force bends the path more sharply, so a higher speed is needed for a stable circular orbit at the smaller radius.

questions.explain: Constant speed, changing direction → changing velocity.

sections.title: Moving sources and red-shift

parts.title: The Doppler effect and red-shift
parts.html:
When a wave source moves relative to an observer, the observed wavelength and frequency change. Moving away: each wave is emitted a little further off than the last, so the waves arrive stretched out — longer wavelength, lower frequency. Moving towards: squashed — shorter wavelength, higher frequency. You hear it in the drop in pitch of a siren as it passes.

Red-shift: light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths than light from the same elements in a laboratory on Earth — the dark lines in its spectrum are shifted towards the red end. So the galaxies are moving away from us. And the more distant the galaxy, the bigger its red-shift, so the faster it is moving away.

The June 2024 scheme (Q1(c)(ii), 3 marks): red-shift means the galaxies are moving away; more distant galaxies have a bigger red-shift; more distant galaxies are moving faster. A question may give the equation $z = \dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}$ (change in wavelength ÷ original wavelength); it is not on the equation list, so it will be supplied. When calculating with it, keep both wavelengths in the same form — both in nm, or both in metres in standard form — the 2022 report's advice (the arithmetic is in T3).

parts.title: Reading a red-shifted spectrum
parts.question: A hydrogen line is at 656 nm in the laboratory and at 668 nm in the light from a galaxy. State what this tells you about the galaxy, and what you would expect for a galaxy twice as far away. (3 marks)
steps: Observation: the line has a longer wavelength than on Earth — it is red-shifted.
Meaning: the galaxy is moving away from us.
Further galaxy: a larger red-shift (the line at a longer wavelength still), because more distant galaxies are moving away faster.

questions.text: A source of waves moves away from an observer. State what happens to the observed wavelength and frequency. (2)
questions.model:
• Wavelength increases (longer).
  • Frequency decreases (lower).

questions.text: State what is meant by red-shift. (1)
questions.model: • The increase in wavelength of light from a source (galaxy) that is moving away — its spectral lines are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.

options: A has a smaller red-shift than B
A has a larger red-shift than B and is moving away faster
questions.explain: Red-shift increases with distance.

questions.text: Describe how the red-shift of light from galaxies depends on their distance from Earth. (2)
questions.model:
• Light from (almost) all galaxies is red-shifted — they are moving away.
  • The further the galaxy, the greater the red-shift (the faster it recedes).

questions.text: A spectral line at 500 nm on Earth appears at 520 nm in light from a galaxy. The red-shift z = (change in wavelength) ÷ (original wavelength). Calculate z.
A star's light is blue-shifted. What does this show?
questions.explain: Towards → shorter wavelength → blue-shift (a few nearby galaxies, e.g. Andromeda, do this).

Describe red-shift in the light from galaxies and how it depends on distance

sections.title: Big Bang, Steady State, and the evidence

parts.title: The two theories and the two pieces of evidence
parts.html:
Big BangSteady State
The Universebegan about 13.8 billion years ago from a very small, very hot, very dense point and has been expanding (and cooling) ever sincehas always existed and always will; it is expanding, but new matter is continually created so it looks the same at all times
Explains red-shift?yes — space is expanding, so galaxies move apartyes — space is expanding, so galaxies move apart
Explains the CMB?yes — predicted it: the leftover radiation from the hot early Universe, stretched to microwaves by the expansionno — gives no reason for it
Statusaccepted modelabandoned

Red-shift → expansion (7.13P): the light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, so they are moving away; the further away a galaxy, the faster it recedes. That is what you see from any point in a space that is expanding everywhere — like dots on an inflating balloon. Running it backwards, everything was once together: a beginning.

The CMB (cosmic microwave background, 7.15P): faint microwave radiation coming from every direction in the sky, at the same temperature everywhere (about 2.7 K). The Big Bang theory predicted it: the early Universe was hot and full of radiation, and the expansion has stretched that radiation to microwave wavelengths. When it was discovered (1964) it matched the prediction; Steady State had no explanation, so the Big Bang became the accepted model — it is the theory with more supporting evidence (7.10P).

The June 2025 6-marker (Q10(c)): Level 3 needs at least one piece of evidence described and linked to the aspect of the Big Bang it supports, and the other identified — red-shift linked to expansion, the CMB (microwaves "across the sky") linked to a definite beginning (a hot early Universe). Isolated statements were Level 1.

parts.title: The 6-mark answer
parts.question: Describe the evidence that supports the Big Bang theory. (6 marks)
steps: Red-shift — observation: light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths than the same light on Earth; the further the galaxy, the bigger the red-shift.
Red-shift — what it shows: the galaxies are moving away, and the more distant ones faster, so the Universe is expanding; traced back, everything was once in one place — a beginning.
CMB — observation: faint microwave radiation is detected coming from all directions in the sky, at almost the same intensity everywhere.
CMB — what it shows: the Big Bang predicted it as the radiation left over from the hot, dense early Universe, stretched to microwaves by the expansion; the Steady State theory could not explain it.
Conclusion: red-shift fits both theories, the CMB fits only the Big Bang, so the Big Bang has more supporting evidence and is the accepted model.

sections.title: The life cycles of stars

parts.title: The two paths
parts.html:
StageWhat is happening
Nebulaa huge cloud of dust and gas (mostly hydrogen); gravity pulls it together
Protostarthe collapsing cloud gets denser and hotter as gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy
Main sequence starthe core is hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium, releasing energy; the star is stable because the outward pressure from the hot gas balances gravity; the Sun is here, for about 10 billion years
Star of similar mass to the Sun
Red giantthe hydrogen in the core runs out; the core contracts and heats, helium fuses into heavier elements, and the outer layers expand and cool (red)
White dwarfthe outer layers drift away; the small, very hot, dense core is left with no fusion, slowly cooling…
Black dwarf…until it no longer glows
Star with a mass much larger than the Sun
Red supergiantas the red giant, but far bigger; fusion makes heavier and heavier elements, up to iron
Supernovathe core collapses suddenly and the star explodes, scattering the elements (and making the ones heavier than iron)
Neutron star or black holethe core left behind is a tiny, incredibly dense neutron star — or, for the most massive stars, a black hole, whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes

The June 2025 report (Q10(a)): the key variable deciding the end of a star is its mass — not its age. "Older stars are more likely to become black holes" was the common wrong answer; the heaviest stars have the shortest lives.

parts.title: A Sun-like star
parts.question: Describe the life cycle of a star of similar mass to the Sun. (4 marks)
steps: Nebula → protostar: gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas together; it gets denser and hotter, forming a protostar.
Main sequence: when the core is hot enough, hydrogen fuses into helium; the star is stable for billions of years, the outward pressure balancing gravity.
Red giant: when the hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and the outer layers expand and cool; helium fuses into heavier elements.
White dwarf → black dwarf: the outer layers are shed, leaving a hot dense core with no fusion that cools into a white dwarf and eventually a black dwarf.

sections.title: How we observe the Universe, and why some telescopes are in space

parts.title: The timeline, and the atmosphere problem
parts.html:
1. Naked eye: for most of history — positions of stars and planets, no detail.
  2. Optical telescopes (Galileo, 1609–10): magnified images — moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus, craters on the Moon. Bigger lenses and mirrors (Newton's reflecting telescope) collect more light, so fainter and more distant objects can be seen.
  3. Photography (1800s): long exposures record far fainter objects than the eye and give a permanent record to measure and compare.
  4. Telescopes for other wavelengths (1930s on): radio, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma telescopes reveal objects and processes invisible in light — cool dust clouds in infrared, black holes' surroundings in X-rays, the CMB in microwaves.
  5. Telescopes in space (Hubble 1990, James Webb 2021): above the atmosphere.
  6. Computers and digital detectors: far more sensitive than film, and able to process huge amounts of data.

Why go above the atmosphere: the atmosphere absorbs most infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, so those can only be observed from space; moving air distorts the light (stars twinkle), blurring images; clouds, dust and light pollution get in the way. In space there is a clear view of every wavelength, day and night. The 2022 report: say that the telescope is in space and why — "candidates stated the location without explaining why it matters".

Disadvantages: very expensive to build and launch; hard or impossible to repair or upgrade; size limited by the rocket.

parts.title: Why in space
parts.question: Explain why some telescopes are placed on satellites rather than on the Earth's surface. (2 marks)
steps: Where: a satellite telescope is above the Earth's atmosphere.

Why: so the light it collects is not absorbed (the atmosphere blocks most infrared, UV and X-rays) or distorted by the air, clouds, dust and light pollution — giving sharper images and access to wavelengths that never reach the ground.

• From the naked eye to telescopes (larger lenses and mirrors collecting more light), and to photography / digital detectors recording fainter objects.
  • From visible light only to telescopes for other wavelengths (radio, infrared, X-ray), and from the ground to telescopes in space.

sections.title: From an Earth-centred to a Sun-centred Solar System

parts.title: Two models and what changed them
parts.html:
Geocentric (Ptolemy, ancient Greece)Heliocentric (Copernicus 1543, Galileo, Kepler)
Centrethe Earth, not movingthe Sun
What orbits whatthe Sun, Moon, planets and stars all circle the Earththe planets, including the Earth, orbit the Sun; the Moon orbits the Earth; the Earth spins once a day
Orbitscircles, with extra circles (epicycles) added to fit the planets' wandering pathsfirst circles, then ellipses (Kepler) once accurate measurements showed circles did not fit
Why believedit matches what you see: the sky turns, the Earth feels stillit is simpler, and it predicts observations the geocentric model cannot

The observations that changed the model — the point the spec wants (7.4P):

  1. Planets sometimes appear to move backwards (retrograde motion). Geocentric models needed epicycles to fake this; in a heliocentric model it happens naturally when the faster-moving Earth overtakes an outer planet.
  2. Galileo's telescope (1609–10) showed four moons orbiting Jupiter — bodies that plainly did not orbit the Earth, so not everything does.
  3. The telescope also showed Venus has phases like the Moon, including gibbous (nearly full) ones — impossible if Venus always lay between the Earth and the Sun, as the geocentric model had it, but expected if Venus goes round the Sun.
  4. Better measurements (Tycho Brahe, Kepler) showed planets move in ellipses, at speeds that change along the orbit; later Newton's gravity explained why.

The general lesson: a model is accepted while it explains the observations; when new, better evidence (here from a new instrument) cannot be explained by the old model but can by a new one, the model changes. The same test decides between the Big Bang and Steady State (T4).

parts.title: The 3-mark 'explain how observations changed the model'
parts.question: Explain how the invention of the telescope led to the geocentric model being replaced by the heliocentric model. (3 marks)
steps: The telescope let Galileo see four moons orbiting Jupiter…
…which showed that not everything orbits the Earth, as the geocentric model claimed; he also saw Venus go through phases, which needs Venus to orbit the Sun.
These observations could not be explained by the Earth-centred model but were predicted by the Sun-centred model, so the evidence supported the heliocentric model and it replaced the old one.

questions.text: Describe the geocentric model of the Solar System. (2)
questions.model:
• The Earth is at the centre and does not move.
  • The Sun, Moon, planets (and stars) all orbit the Earth.

questions.text: Describe the heliocentric model of the Solar System. (2)
questions.model:
• The Sun is at the centre.
  • The planets, including the Earth, orbit the Sun (in ellipses); the Moon orbits the Earth.

questions.text: Which observation showed that not everything orbits the Earth?
options: The Sun rising in the east
questions.explain: Galileo's four moons of Jupiter plainly circled Jupiter, not the Earth.

questions.text: Explain why the phases of Venus supported the heliocentric model. (2)
questions.model:
• Venus was seen to show a full set of phases, including nearly full…
  • …which is only possible if Venus orbits the Sun and is sometimes on the far side of it from the Earth — the geocentric model could not produce this.

questions.text: Explain why scientists replace one model with another. (2)
questions.model:
• New observations (often from new instruments) are made that the old model cannot explain…
  • …while the new model explains or predicts them, so it has more supporting evidence.

questions.text: In the heliocentric model, the shape of a planet's orbit is…
questions.explain: Kepler showed the orbits are ellipses; for the planets they are very close to circles.

checklist: Describe the geocentric and heliocentric models
Explain how observations, especially with the telescope, led to the Sun-centred model
Explain why a scientific model is changed

sections.title: Explaining orbits: the words the marks are on

parts.title: Three chains
parts.html:
Chain 1 — constant speed but accelerating: velocity is a vector → the direction of motion is continuously changing → so the velocity is changing → a changing velocity is an acceleration → it needs a resultant force → that force is gravity, acting towards the centre. Trap: "it is accelerating because it is speeding up" — it is not; and "centripetal force" on its own was ignored in June 2024 — name the force (gravity) and its direction.

Chain 2 — radius and speed: closer to the central body → stronger gravitational force → a tighter turn is needed → higher speed for a stable orbit. The spec's wording (7.7P): if the speed of an orbiting body changes, the radius of its orbit must change too — faster → smaller orbit; slower → larger orbit. Trap: students write "closer orbits are slower because they have less distance to travel". Less distance per orbit is why the period is shorter, but the speed is higher.

Chain 3 — comets: highly elliptical orbit → gravitational force from the Sun is stronger when closer → the comet speeds up as it falls towards the Sun (gravitational potential store → kinetic store) and slows as it climbs away → fastest at the closest point, slowest at the furthest. Trap: a comet's orbit is not a circle, so its speed is not constant, unlike a planet's.

Geostationary explained: there is only one height (about 36 000 km) at which the orbital period is exactly 24 hours; placed there above the equator, moving the same way the Earth turns, a satellite stays over one point. Lower → period shorter → it drifts ahead of the ground.

parts.title: Radius and speed, both ways
parts.question: Satellite A orbits the Earth at a height of 400 km; satellite B at 20 000 km. (a) State which satellite moves faster. (b) Explain your answer. (c) A third satellite, C, is in a stable orbit at a higher speed than A. State how the radius of C's orbit compares with A's. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Satellite A (the lower one).
(b) A is closer to the Earth, so the gravitational force on each kilogram is stronger; a stronger force bends the path more sharply, which needs a higher speed for a stable circular orbit.
(c) C's orbit has a smaller radius than A's: a stable orbit at a higher speed needs the stronger gravity found closer in. (If a body's speed changes, the radius of its stable orbit must change too.)

questions.text: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Explain why there must be a resultant force on it, and state what provides the force. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VectorVelocity is a vector; the satellite's direction is continuously changing, so its velocity is changing.
2AccelerationA change in velocity is an acceleration, and an acceleration needs a resultant force.
3ForceThe force is gravity, acting towards the centre of the Earth.

questions.text: A student says: "The Moon's velocity is constant because its speed is constant." Why is this wrong?
options: Velocity includes direction, and the Moon's direction keeps changing
Velocity and speed are the same
questions.explain: Steady speed round a circle is a changing velocity.

questions.text: Explain why a planet closer to the Sun must move faster than one further away to stay in a stable orbit. (2)
questions.model:
• Closer to the Sun the gravitational force is stronger.
  • A stronger force makes the path curve more tightly, so a higher speed is needed to keep a stable (circular) orbit of that smaller radius.

questions.text: A comet's orbit is highly elliptical. Describe how its speed changes during one orbit and explain why. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1PatternIt is fastest when nearest the Sun and slowest when furthest away.
2Falling inAs it approaches the Sun the gravitational force increases and does work on it: energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store.
3Climbing outMoving away, gravity slows it: kinetic → gravitational potential.

questions.text: A satellite is moved from a high orbit to a lower one. Its speed…
questions.explain: Smaller radius → stronger gravity → faster.

questions.text: Explain why a geostationary satellite must be placed at one particular height. (2)
questions.model:
• Its period must be 24 hours to match the Earth's rotation, so that it stays above the same point.
  • The orbital speed (and so the period) depends on the radius, so only one height gives a 24-hour period (lower → faster → shorter period).

sections.title: The red-shift argument, step by step

parts.title: The chain, and the exam traps
parts.html:
The June 2022 Paper 1H question (Q6) gave the spectra of two galaxies and asked students to explain how they showed the Universe is expanding. The scheme:

MarkWhat to write
1The lines in the more distant galaxy's spectrum are at longer wavelengths — it has the greater red-shift.
2Greater red-shift means it is moving away faster; so more distant galaxies move away faster, which is what an expanding Universe looks like.

Spell out each arrow. Common losses: saying "the galaxy is red-shifted" without saying what that shows; saying "moving away" without the distance–speed link; saying "expanding" with no evidence. Writing "the light gets redder" is not the same as "the wavelength is longer".

Why expansion: if every galaxy is moving away from us, and the further ones faster, either we are at the centre of a huge explosion (we are not — every galaxy sees the same thing) or space itself is stretching, carrying all the galaxies apart. Dots on a balloon being inflated: every dot sees every other move away, the more distant ones faster.

Why red-shift does not settle the argument: both the Big Bang and the Steady State theory describe an expanding Universe, so both predict red-shift. Red-shift is evidence for expansion, not for the Big Bang alone. What decided it was the CMB (T4).

The calculations (if a question supplies the equations): $z = \dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}$, and recession velocity $v = z \times c$ with $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s. The 2022 report: candidates mixed standard form with ordinary numbers (656 nm with 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m) and lost the arithmetic; keep every wavelength in the same form, and use the "show that" value in the next part if there is one.

parts.title: Two spectra
parts.question: The spectrum of light from galaxy X shows a hydrogen line at 660 nm; from galaxy Y the same line is at 700 nm. In the laboratory the line is at 656 nm. Explain which galaxy is further from Earth and how these observations support the idea of an expanding Universe. (4 marks)
steps: Both lines are at longer wavelengths than 656 nm, so both galaxies are red-shifted and moving away from us.
Y's line is shifted more (44 nm against 4 nm), so Y has the greater red-shift and is moving away faster.
The more distant a galaxy, the greater its red-shift — so Y is further away.
More distant galaxies receding faster is what is seen when space itself is expanding, carrying the galaxies apart.

questions.text: A spectral line is at 486 nm in the laboratory. In the light from galaxy P it is at 490 nm; from galaxy Q it is at 510 nm.

parts.text: State which galaxy is further from Earth. (1)

parts.model:
• Q's line has the longer wavelength / bigger red-shift (24 nm against 4 nm), so Q is moving away faster…
  • …and more distant galaxies have the bigger red-shift (move away faster).

parts.text: The red-shift z = (change in wavelength) ÷ (original wavelength). Calculate z for galaxy Q.

questions.text: Explain how the red-shift of light from distant galaxies provides evidence that the Universe is expanding. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ObservationThe light from distant galaxies is red-shifted: its wavelength is longer than from the same source on Earth.
2MeaningSo the galaxies are moving away from us.
3PatternThe more distant the galaxy the greater the red-shift, so the faster it recedes — every galaxy moving apart from every other is an expanding Universe.

questions.text: Why does red-shift NOT prove the Big Bang theory on its own?
options: The Steady State theory also describes an expanding Universe and so also predicts red-shift
questions.explain: Red-shift is evidence for expansion, which both theories include.

questions.text: A galaxy has a red-shift $z = 0.02$. Its recession velocity is given by $v = z \times c$, where $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s. Calculate v.
A student writes: "Red-shift means the galaxies are moving away from the Earth, so the Earth is at the centre of the Universe." Explain why the conclusion is wrong. (2)
questions.model:
• If space itself is expanding, every galaxy moves away from every other — an observer in any galaxy sees the same red-shift pattern.
  • So the observation does not put the Earth at a centre; there is no centre (the balloon analogy).

questions.text: The light from a distant galaxy shows a hydrogen line at a longer wavelength than in the laboratory. What is the correct phrase for the mark?
options: "The wavelength has increased — the light is red-shifted — so the galaxy is moving away"
questions.explain: Name the change in wavelength and what it shows.

checklist: Compare two spectra and say which galaxy is further away and why
Write the full chain from observation to 'the Universe is expanding'
Explain why red-shift alone does not decide between Big Bang and Steady State
sections.blurb: Red-shift questions give you two spectra, or a table of galaxies, and ask what they show. The marks are on a fixed chain: longer wavelength → moving away → more distant means faster → expanding. Miss a link and the mark goes.

sections.title: Why the CMB decided between the two theories

parts.title: The argument, in the order the marks want it
parts.html:
1. Two theories, both with expansion. Big Bang: the Universe began from a tiny, hot, dense point and has expanded and cooled since. Steady State: it has always existed, expanding, with new matter continually created to fill the gaps, so it looks the same for ever.
  2. Red-shift fits both. Both say space is expanding, so both predict galaxies receding, faster when further. Red-shift cannot choose between them.
  3. The Big Bang made a prediction. If the early Universe was hot and dense, it was full of high-energy radiation. As space expanded, that radiation was stretched to longer wavelengths (red-shifted enormously) — it should now be faint microwaves, coming equally from every direction, with a temperature a few degrees above absolute zero.
  4. The prediction was found. In 1964 Penzias and Wilson detected microwave radiation from all directions in the sky — the cosmic microwave background — at about 2.7 K, just as predicted.
  5. Steady State had no explanation. A Universe that has always looked the same has no hot early phase to leave radiation behind. The theory could not account for the CMB.
  6. So the Big Bang became the accepted model (7.10P): it is the theory with more supporting evidence — both red-shift and the CMB — and it made a prediction that was confirmed. That is how a scientific model is judged.

The June 2025 levels (Q10(c), 6 marks): Level 3 — at least one piece of evidence described and linked to the aspect of the theory it supports (the CMB "across the sky" → a hot early Universe, a definite beginning; red-shift → expansion), with the other identified; Level 1 — isolated statements ("there is red-shift", "there is CMB"). The report: students knew the names of the evidence but did not say what each showed.

Word traps: the CMB is microwave radiation, not light and not "radio waves from the Big Bang"; it comes from all directions, not from one place; and the Big Bang was not an explosion in space — it was the start of the expansion of space.

parts.title: Comparing the theories (6 marks)
parts.question: Scientists once supported two theories of the Universe, the Big Bang and the Steady State. Explain how evidence led to the Big Bang theory becoming the accepted theory. (6 marks)
steps: Both theories say the Universe is expanding; the Big Bang says it began from a tiny, hot, dense point, the Steady State says it has always existed with new matter continually created.
Red-shift: light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths, more so the more distant the galaxy, showing galaxies are moving apart — the Universe is expanding. This supports both theories.
The Big Bang theory predicted that radiation left over from the hot early Universe should still be detectable, stretched by the expansion to microwave wavelengths and coming from all directions.
The cosmic microwave background was then discovered, matching that prediction — evidence for a hot, dense beginning.
The Steady State theory could not explain the CMB, because it has no hot early Universe.
So the Big Bang theory has more supporting evidence (red-shift and the CMB) and a confirmed prediction, and it became the accepted model.

questions.text: Describe what the cosmic microwave background radiation is. (2)
questions.model:
• Microwave radiation detected coming from all directions in space (at the same temperature, about 2.7 K).
  • It is the radiation left over from the hot early Universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths by the expansion.

questions.text: Explain why the CMB supports the Big Bang theory. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1PredictionThe Big Bang theory says the early Universe was hot and dense and full of radiation.
2StretchingAs the Universe expanded, that radiation was stretched to longer (microwave) wavelengths and should be seen coming from everywhere.
3MatchMicrowave radiation is detected from all directions, as predicted — so it is evidence for a hot beginning.

questions.text: Explain why the discovery of the CMB led scientists to reject the Steady State theory. (2)
questions.model:
• The Steady State theory says the Universe has always existed and looked the same, with no hot early phase…
  • …so it cannot explain where the CMB comes from, while the Big Bang theory predicted it.

questions.text: Which statement about the Big Bang is correct?
options: It was an explosion of matter into empty space
It was the start of the expansion of space itself, from a tiny, hot, dense state
It happened at the centre of the Universe
questions.explain: Space itself expanded; there is no centre.

questions.text: A theory makes a prediction that is later observed. Explain why this makes scientists more confident in the theory. (2)
questions.model:
• The observation was not known when the theory was made, so the theory was not simply built to fit it.
  • The theory explains something a rival theory cannot — it has more supporting evidence, so it becomes the accepted model.

questions.text: A student's 6-mark answer says: "There is red-shift. There is CMB. So the Big Bang is right." Which level would this reach?
options: Level 1 — isolated statements with no links
questions.explain: Each piece of evidence must be described and linked to what it shows.

checklist: Describe what the CMB is and where it comes from in the Big Bang picture
Explain why the CMB supports the Big Bang but not the Steady State theory
Describe how a theory becomes the accepted one

sections.title: How a star forms, stays stable, and stops

parts.title: Gravity versus pressure
parts.html:
StageGravityOutward pressureResult
Nebula → protostarpulls the gas and dust togethersmallthe cloud collapses; compressing it makes it denser and hotter (gravitational potential → thermal)
Fusion startsstill pulling incore hot enough (millions of °C) for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium, releasing energythe energy heats the gas, whose pressure pushes outwards
Main sequenceinwardoutward, from the hot gasbalanced — the star is stable and the same size for billions of years
Hydrogen runs outwins in the corefallsthe core contracts and heats until helium fuses; the extra energy pushes the outer layers out — a red giant (or supergiant)
Fuel gone (Sun-like)winsnone — no fusionthe core shrinks to a white dwarf, which slowly cools
Fuel gone (massive)wins suddenlynonethe core collapses in seconds — supernova; the remnant is a neutron star or, if gravity is strong enough to beat everything, a black hole

The June 2023 scheme (Q4(d), explaining how a protostar becomes a main sequence star): gravity causes the cloud to collapse; the collapse raises the temperature until fusion starts; the star is stable because gravity and the outward pressure from fusion balance. "Fission" instead of fusion scored nothing — fusion joins small nuclei, fission splits large ones. Say nuclei (hydrogen nuclei fuse), not "atoms" or "particles".

parts.title: The 3-mark stability explanation
parts.question: Explain how a protostar becomes a main sequence star, and why a main sequence star remains the same size for billions of years. (3 marks)
steps: Gravity pulls the gas and dust of the protostar inwards, compressing it and making the core hotter and denser.
When the core is hot enough, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy — the star is now a main sequence star.
It stays the same size because the outward pressure of the hot gas, kept up by fusion, balances the inward force of gravity.

questions.text: Explain how a nebula becomes a protostar. (2)
questions.model:
• Gravity pulls the particles of gas and dust together, so the cloud collapses and becomes denser.
  • Compressing the gas transfers energy to its thermal store: it gets hotter (but fusion has not yet started).

questions.text: Explain why a main sequence star is stable. (2)
questions.model:
• Fusion of hydrogen into helium releases energy, so the hot gas exerts an outward pressure.
  • This outward pressure balances the inward pull of gravity, so the star neither expands nor collapses.

questions.text: What process releases the energy in a main sequence star?
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium
questions.explain: Fusion: small nuclei join. Fission is splitting, and it is not what powers stars.

questions.text: Explain what happens to a star like the Sun when the hydrogen in its core runs out. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Balance lostFusion in the core slows, so the outward pressure falls and gravity wins: the core contracts and gets hotter.
2New fusionThe core becomes hot enough for helium to fuse into heavier elements.
3ExpansionThe extra energy pushes the outer layers outwards; they expand and cool — the star becomes a red giant.

questions.text: Explain why a star much more massive than the Sun ends in a supernova while the Sun will not. (2)
questions.model:
• A more massive star has much stronger gravity, so when fusion stops its core collapses suddenly and violently…
  • …and the collapse blows the outer layers away in a supernova; the Sun's gravity is too weak for this, so its core just shrinks to a white dwarf.

questions.text: A student writes: "The star is stable because gravity is balanced by nuclear fission." What is wrong?
options: Stars are powered by fusion, not fission
questions.explain: Fusion joins hydrogen nuclei; fission splits heavy nuclei and does not happen in stars.

checklist: Explain how gravity forms a protostar and starts fusion
Explain the balance that keeps a main sequence star stable
Explain what changes when the hydrogen runs out, for both masses of star
sections.blurb: The questions are 'explain how a star forms', 'explain why a main sequence star is stable' and 'explain what happens when the fuel runs out'. All three are the same two forces: gravity pulling in, the pressure of hot gas pushing out.

sections.title: Telescopes in space and telescopes for other wavelengths
equations: \text{above the atmosphere: no absorption, no distortion}

parts.title: The arguments and their reasons
parts.html:
Advantage of a space telescopeBecause…
can observe infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma raysthe atmosphere absorbs most of these, so they never reach the ground
sharper imagesno distortion (twinkling) from moving air of varying density refracting the light
sees fainter objectsno light pollution from towns, no scattered daylight, no clouds or dust — observations possible all the time
DisadvantageBecause…
very expensivelaunching a telescope into orbit costs far more than building one on a mountain
hard to repair or upgradeastronauts or robots have to reach it (Hubble was serviced; Webb, 1.5 million km away, cannot be)
size limitedit must fit in a rocket, so the mirror is smaller than the biggest ground telescopes (Webb's unfolds)

The 2022 report (Q6(c)): the question asked why some telescopes are on satellites; many "stated the location without explaining why it matters". Write where (above the atmosphere) and the consequence (no absorption / distortion / pollution).

Other wavelengths (and why bother): objects emit at wavelengths set by their temperature and processes — cool dust and gas clouds where stars form glow in infrared; very hot gas round black holes and in supernova remnants gives X-rays; radio telescopes see through dust and detect the CMB (microwaves) and pulsars; radio and some infrared pass through the atmosphere, so those telescopes can be on the ground (radio dishes are huge for that reason). Each wavelength reveals something the others cannot, so a complete picture needs them all.

parts.title: State and explain
parts.question: The James Webb Space Telescope observes infrared radiation from an orbit far from the Earth. (a) Explain why it had to be placed in space. (b) Give two disadvantages of placing a telescope in space. (4 marks)
steps: (a) The Earth's atmosphere absorbs most infrared radiation, so a ground telescope would receive very little…
…above the atmosphere all the infrared reaches the telescope, undistorted by the air and unaffected by clouds and light pollution.
(b) It is very expensive to build and launch…
…and it cannot be repaired or upgraded if something goes wrong (and its size is limited by the rocket).

questions.text: Explain one advantage of placing an optical telescope in orbit around the Earth. (2)
questions.model:
• It is above the atmosphere…
  • …so the light is not distorted by moving air (or dimmed by clouds / light pollution), giving sharper, clearer images.

questions.text: Explain why an X-ray telescope cannot be used on the ground. (2)
questions.model:
• X-rays from space are absorbed by the atmosphere…
  • …so they do not reach the ground — the telescope must be above the atmosphere to detect them.

questions.text: Which type of telescope works well on the ground because its waves pass through the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Radio waves (and visible light) pass through the atmosphere; most IR, UV, X and gamma do not.

questions.text: Give two disadvantages of space telescopes compared with ground-based telescopes. (2)
questions.model:
• Much more expensive (launch costs).
  • Difficult or impossible to repair, maintain or upgrade; size limited by the rocket.

  • So the infrared telescope reveals objects and detail that a visible-light telescope cannot see.

sections.title: Weight and g the hard way: ratios, rearranging and the balance trap

parts.title: Three routes and a trap
parts.html:
Route 1 — via the mass. Weight on Earth → mass ($m = W \div 10$) → weight elsewhere ($W = m \times g$). The mass is the bridge: it never changes.

Route 2 — ratios. Weight is proportional to $g$ for a fixed mass, so if $g_{\text{Moon}}$ is 1/6 of Earth's, every weight on the Moon is 1/6 of its Earth value: 600 N → 100 N, no mass needed. "g on Mars is 0.38 times g on Earth" → multiply Earth weights by 0.38.

Route 3 — finding g. Drop or weigh a known mass: $g = W \div m$. From a newton meter reading of 7.4 N for a 2 kg mass on Mars, $g = 3.7$ N/kg. Unit N/kg (the same as m/s², the acceleration of free fall there).

The balance trap. A newton meter / spring balance measures the force pulling the spring — the weight — so it reads less on the Moon. A beam balance (scales with standard masses on the other side) compares the pull of gravity on two masses at the same place; both are reduced by the same factor, so it balances at the same mass as on Earth. Bathroom scales are spring balances marked in kg assuming Earth's $g$: on the Moon they would read a sixth of your mass — wrongly.

Why g differs (the explain mark): $g$ at a surface depends on the body's mass and its radius; a more massive body pulls harder, a larger radius puts the surface further from the centre and weakens the pull. In orbit $g$ is smaller but not zero — astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together, not because there is no gravity.

parts.title: Via the mass, then ratios
parts.question: An astronaut weighs 720 N on Earth ($g = 10$ N/kg). (a) Calculate his weight on the Moon ($g = 1.6$ N/kg). (b) On Mars g is 0.38 times its value on Earth. Calculate his weight on Mars without finding his mass again.
steps: (a) Mass: $m = \dfrac{W}{g} = \dfrac{720}{10} = 72$ kg.
On the Moon: $W = m \times g = 72 \times 1.6 = 115$ N (3 s.f.).
(b) Weight is proportional to $g$ for the same mass: $W_{\text{Mars}} = 0.38 \times 720 = 274$ N (3 s.f.).

facts.q: What does the Solar System consist of?
facts.a: The Sun, eight planets with their natural satellites (moons), dwarf planets, asteroids and comets (plus artificial satellites).

facts.q: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun.
facts.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

facts.q: What is a dwarf planet? Give an example.
facts.a: A body that orbits the Sun and is round but has not cleared its orbit of other objects — Pluto, Ceres, Eris.

facts.q: Where is the asteroid belt?
facts.a: Between Mars and Jupiter.

facts.q: Which four planets are small and rocky, and which four are gas giants?
facts.a: Rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars. Gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

facts.q: What is the equation for weight?
facts.a: $W = m \times g$ (weight = mass × gravitational field strength).

facts.q: Does your mass change on the Moon? Does your weight?
facts.a: Mass: no, it is the same everywhere. Weight: yes, it is about a sixth, because g on the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg.

facts.q: What does g at the surface of a body depend on?
facts.a: The body's mass (more mass → larger g) and its radius (larger radius → smaller g).

facts.q: g on the Earth, Moon, Mars and Jupiter?
facts.a: Earth 10 N/kg; Moon 1.6 N/kg; Mars 3.7 N/kg; Jupiter 25 N/kg.

facts.q: Which reads differently on the Moon: a newton meter or a beam balance?
facts.a: The newton meter (it measures weight). The beam balance compares masses and reads the same.

facts.q: Describe the orbits of the planets.
facts.a: Near-circular (slightly elliptical) orbits around the Sun, roughly in one plane, at almost constant speed.

facts.q: Describe the orbit of a comet.
facts.a: Highly elliptical around the Sun; fastest when closest to the Sun, slowest when furthest.

facts.q: What does a moon (natural satellite) orbit?
facts.a: A planet.

facts.q: What is a geostationary orbit, and what is it used for?
facts.a: An orbit above the equator with a 24-hour period, so the satellite stays over one point — TV and communications.

facts.q: What is a low polar orbit used for, and why?
facts.a: Weather, imaging and mapping: the satellite passes over the poles every ~90 min while the Earth turns beneath it, so it covers the whole surface.

facts.q: Why does a comet speed up near the Sun?
facts.a: The Sun's gravitational force increases as it gets closer; energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store.

facts.q: What force keeps a satellite in orbit?
facts.a: Gravity (the Earth's gravitational pull), acting towards the centre of the Earth.

facts.q: A planet in a circular orbit has constant speed. Is its velocity constant?
facts.a: No — its direction is continuously changing, so its velocity is changing (velocity is a vector).

facts.q: Why is a body in a circular orbit accelerating?
facts.a: Its velocity is changing (direction changes continuously); the acceleration is towards the centre, caused by gravity.

facts.q: In which direction does gravity act on an orbiting body, relative to its velocity?
facts.a: Towards the centre — at right angles to the velocity — so it changes the direction but not the speed.

facts.q: How are orbital radius and orbital speed linked for a stable orbit?
facts.a: Smaller radius → stronger gravity → higher speed needed. So if an orbiting body's speed changes, its orbital radius must change too (spec 7.7P).

facts.q: Why does Mercury orbit faster than Neptune?
facts.a: It is much closer to the Sun, so the gravitational force on it is stronger and a higher speed is needed for a stable orbit.

facts.q: A wave source moves away from you. What happens to the observed wavelength and frequency?
facts.a: Wavelength increases; frequency decreases.

facts.q: A wave source moves towards you. What happens to the observed wavelength and frequency?
facts.a: Wavelength decreases; frequency increases (blue-shift for light).

facts.q: What is red-shift?
facts.a: The increase in wavelength of light from a source moving away — spectral lines shifted towards the red end.

facts.q: How does a galaxy's red-shift depend on its distance?
facts.a: The more distant the galaxy, the greater its red-shift — so the faster it is moving away.

facts.q: What does the red-shift of galaxies tell us about them?
facts.a: They are moving away from us; more distant ones faster.

facts.q: Describe the Big Bang theory.
facts.a: The Universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a very small, hot, dense point and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

facts.q: Describe the Steady State theory.
facts.a: The Universe has always existed and always will; it expands, but new matter is continually created so it always looks the same.

facts.q: What two pieces of evidence support the Big Bang?
facts.a: Red-shift of galaxies (expansion) and the cosmic microwave background (a hot beginning).

facts.q: Which evidence fits both theories, and which fits only the Big Bang?
facts.a: Red-shift fits both (both have expansion); the CMB fits only the Big Bang.

facts.q: What is the CMB?
facts.a: Cosmic microwave background: microwave radiation from all directions in space, left over from the hot early Universe and stretched by the expansion.

facts.q: Why did the Big Bang become the accepted theory?
facts.a: It predicted the CMB, which was then discovered; the Steady State theory could not explain it — so the Big Bang has more supporting evidence.

facts.q: How does red-shift show the Universe is expanding?
facts.a: All distant galaxies are moving away, and the further they are the faster — exactly what is seen if space itself is expanding everywhere.

facts.q: Life cycle of a star like the Sun?
facts.a: Nebula → protostar → main sequence star → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.

facts.q: Life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun?
facts.a: Nebula → protostar → main sequence star → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

facts.q: What decides how a star ends its life?
facts.a: Its mass (not its age).

facts.q: What is a nebula?
facts.a: A cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars form.

facts.q: What happens in a protostar?
facts.a: Gravity pulls the cloud together; it becomes denser and hotter, but fusion has not yet started.

facts.q: What happens in a main sequence star?
facts.a: Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing energy; the star is stable.

facts.q: What is a red giant?
facts.a: A star whose core hydrogen has run out: the core contracts and heats, helium fuses, and the outer layers expand and cool.

facts.q: What is a white dwarf?
facts.a: The small, very hot, dense core left after a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers; no fusion; slowly cooling.

facts.q: What is a supernova?
facts.a: The explosion of a massive star when its core collapses at the end of its life.

facts.q: What is left after a supernova?
facts.a: A neutron star — or a black hole if the star was massive enough.

facts.q: What is a black hole?
facts.a: The remnant of the most massive stars; gravity so strong that not even light can escape.

facts.q: Why is a main sequence star stable?
facts.a: The outward pressure of the hot gas (from fusion) balances the inward pull of gravity.

facts.q: How does a protostar become a main sequence star?
facts.a: Gravity collapses the cloud, raising the temperature until hydrogen nuclei fuse; then gravity and the outward pressure balance.

facts.q: Fusion or fission in stars?
facts.a: Fusion — small nuclei (hydrogen) join to make helium. Fission (splitting large nuclei) does not power stars.

facts.q: Why does a star become a red giant when its hydrogen runs out?
facts.a: The core contracts and heats until helium fuses; the extra energy pushes the outer layers out, which expand and cool.

facts.q: How have methods of observing the Universe changed?
facts.a: Naked eye → optical telescopes (bigger lenses and mirrors) → photography → telescopes for other wavelengths (radio, IR, X-ray) → telescopes in space → digital detectors and computers.

facts.q: Why are some telescopes placed in space?
facts.a: Above the atmosphere there is no absorption of IR, UV and X-rays, no distortion by moving air, and no clouds or light pollution — sharper images, all wavelengths.

facts.q: Give two disadvantages of a space telescope.
facts.a: Very expensive to build and launch; hard or impossible to repair or upgrade (and size limited by the rocket).

facts.q: Which wavelengths does the atmosphere block?
facts.a: Most infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Visible light and radio waves get through.

facts.q: Why use telescopes for wavelengths other than light?
facts.a: Different objects emit at different wavelengths: cool dust in infrared, very hot gas in X-rays; radio sees through dust. Each reveals what the others cannot.

facts.q: What did Galileo's telescope show, and why did it matter?
facts.a: Four moons orbiting Jupiter and the phases of Venus — things that could not be explained by an Earth-centred model.

facts.q: What is the geocentric model?
facts.a: The Earth at the centre, not moving; the Sun, Moon, planets and stars orbit the Earth.

facts.q: What is the heliocentric model?
facts.a: The Sun at the centre; the planets, including the Earth, orbit the Sun in ellipses; the Moon orbits the Earth.

facts.q: Why do scientists replace one model with another?
facts.a: New observations that the old model cannot explain but the new model can — the new model has more supporting evidence.

facts.q: The red-shift chain for the marks?
facts.a: Lines at longer wavelength → red-shifted → moving away → more distant galaxies have bigger red-shift so move faster → the Universe is expanding.

facts.q: Why does red-shift alone not prove the Big Bang?
facts.a: Both the Big Bang and the Steady State theory describe an expanding Universe, so both predict red-shift.

facts.q: What does Level 3 need in the 6-mark Big Bang evidence question?
facts.a: At least one piece of evidence described AND linked to what it shows (CMB → hot beginning; red-shift → expansion), the other identified. Isolated statements are Level 1.

facts.q: Three word traps about the Big Bang and CMB?
facts.a: CMB is microwaves (not light or radio); it comes from all directions (not one place); the Big Bang was the expansion of space, not an explosion in space.

facts.q: 'Telescopes are on satellites because they are in space' — why no marks?
facts.a: It gives the location but not the reason: say the atmosphere absorbs or distorts the radiation.

facts.q: Convert a weight on Earth to a weight on the Moon.
facts.a: Mass first ($m = W \div 10$), then $W = m \times 1.6$. Or use the ratio: Moon weight = Earth weight × 1.6/10.

facts.q: Why do astronauts in the ISS float, when g there is about 8.7 N/kg?
facts.a: They and the station are falling towards the Earth together, so nothing pushes up on them — gravity is still acting and keeps them in orbit.

facts.q: State what is meant by: natural satellite.
facts.a: A body that orbits a planet (a moon).

facts.q: State what is meant by: artificial satellite.
facts.a: A man-made object placed in orbit around the Earth (or another body).

facts.q: State what is meant by: dwarf planet.
facts.a: A body that orbits the Sun and is round but has not cleared its orbit of other objects.

facts.q: State what is meant by: comet.
facts.a: An icy body in a highly elliptical orbit around the Sun, fastest when nearest the Sun.

facts.q: State what is meant by: orbit.
facts.a: The path of one body around another, held by gravity.

facts.q: State what is meant by: geostationary orbit.
facts.a: An orbit above the equator with a period of 24 hours, so the satellite stays over the same point.

facts.q: State what is meant by: gravitational field strength g.
facts.a: The force of gravity per kilogram at a place, in N/kg; it depends on the body's mass and radius.

facts.q: State what is meant by: red-shift.
facts.a: The increase in wavelength of light from a source moving away — spectral lines shifted towards the red end.

facts.q: State what is meant by: cosmic microwave background (cmb).
facts.a: Microwave radiation coming from all directions in space — left over from the hot early Universe.

facts.q: State what is meant by: big bang theory.
facts.a: The Universe began from a very small, hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since.

facts.q: State what is meant by: steady state theory.
facts.a: The Universe has always existed, expanding while new matter is created so it always looks the same.

facts.q: State what is meant by: nebula.
facts.a: A cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars form.

facts.q: State what is meant by: protostar.
facts.a: A collapsing cloud that is heating up under gravity but has not yet started fusion.

facts.q: State what is meant by: main sequence star.
facts.a: A star in the stable stage, fusing hydrogen into helium, with outward pressure balancing gravity.

facts.q: State what is meant by: red giant.
facts.a: A star whose core hydrogen has run out: the outer layers expand and cool.

facts.q: State what is meant by: white dwarf.
facts.a: The small, hot, dense core left by a Sun-like star, with no fusion, slowly cooling.

facts.q: State what is meant by: supernova.
facts.a: The explosion of a massive star at the end of its life.

facts.q: State what is meant by: neutron star.
facts.a: The tiny, extremely dense core left after a supernova.

facts.q: State what is meant by: black hole.
facts.a: The remnant of the most massive stars: gravity so strong that not even light can escape.

types.name: Weight on other bodies: W = m × g
equations: g: Earth 10 N/kg, Moon 1.6 N/kg, Mars 3.7 N/kg, Jupiter 25 N/kg
types.method: Weight is the force of gravity on a mass: W = m × g. The mass of an object is the same everywhere; its weight changes because g — the gravitational field strength — is different on each body (it depends on the body's mass and radius). Use the g the question gives for that body. To find g from a weight, g = W ÷ m; to find the mass from a weight on another body, m = W ÷ g for that body, and that mass is the same back on Earth.
commonErrors: Using Earth's g for a weight on the Moon or Mars
Saying the mass changes on the Moon — only the weight changes
Giving the unit of g as N (it is N/kg) or of weight as kg (it is N)
Dividing by the wrong g when converting a Moon weight back to an Earth weight

steps: Known: m = 80 kg, g (Moon) = 1.6 N/kg. Unknown: W.

W = 128 N (on Earth it would be 800 N; her mass is 80 kg in both places)
